### Describe the bug

`dotnet watch` crashes with an unhandled `NullReferenceException` (exit code 134) when re-evaluating a project fails and then any watched file changes. It should report the error and wait for a fix, and it does print `Fix the error to continue or press Ctrl+C to exit.` But the next file event kills it, and the app it started keeps running without it.

We hit this regularly in a real project. A script replaced the contents of an ASP.NET Core project's `wwwroot` while `dotnet watch` was running. The added files triggered a re-evaluation, that build failed because files were still being copied, and the next file event crashed the watcher.

### Steps to reproduce

Minimal repro: https://github.com/haagOS/dotnet-watch-nre-repro

```bash
git clone https://github.com/haagOS/dotnet-watch-nre-repro
cd dotnet-watch-nre-repro
./repro.sh
```

It is a console app whose `.csproj` has one extra target that fails the build while a file named `break-evaluation` exists. The script:

1. Starts `dotnet watch run`.
2. Creates `break-evaluation`. Adding a file makes `dotnet watch` re-evaluate the project, and that build fails. `dotnet watch` prints `Fix the error to continue or press Ctrl+C to exit.`
3. Deletes `break-evaluation`.

It reproduces every time (3 of 3 runs).

### Expected behavior

`dotnet watch` notices the change, re-evaluates the project, and continues.

### Actual behavior

`dotnet watch` exits with code 134:

```
dotnet watch ⌚ File added: ./break-evaluation
dotnet watch ⌚ Loading projects ...
dotnet watch ❌ Failed to build project '.../Repro.csproj'.
dotnet watch 🔨 .../Repro.csproj(13,5): error : break-evaluation exists: failing on purpose.
dotnet watch ⌚ Fix the error to continue or press Ctrl+C to exit.
Unhandled exception. System.NullReferenceException: Object reference not set to an instance of an object.
   at Microsoft.DotNet.Watch.HotReloadDotNetWatcher.AcceptChange(ChangedPath change, EvaluationResult evaluationResult)
   at Microsoft.DotNet.Watch.HotReloadDotNetWatcher.<>c__DisplayClass13_3.<WatchAsync>g__FileChangedCallback|1(ChangedPath change)
   at Microsoft.DotNet.Watch.FileWatcher.WatcherChangedHandler(Object sender, ChangedPath change)
   at Microsoft.DotNet.Watch.DirectoryWatcher.NotifyChange(String fullPath, ChangeKind kind)
   at Microsoft.DotNet.Watch.EventBasedDirectoryWatcher.WatcherDeletedHandler(Object sender, FileSystemEventArgs e)
   at System.IO.FileSystemWatcher.NotifyFileSystemEventArgs(WatcherChangeTypes changeType, ReadOnlySpan`1 name)
   at System.IO.FileSystemWatcher.RunningInstance.ProcessEvents(...)
   at System.IO.FileSystemWatcher.RunningInstance.<>c__DisplayClass14_0.<FileSystemEventCallback>b__0(Object o)
   at System.Threading.ExecutionContext.RunInternal(ExecutionContext executionContext, ContextCallback callback, Object state)
```

Any file event triggers the crash. In some runs the stack shows `WatcherAddedHandler` instead of `WatcherDeletedHandler`.

The app started by `dotnet watch` is not stopped and keeps running after `dotnet watch` exits.

**Cause, from reading the v10.0.401 source:**

- [`FileChangedCallback`](https://github.com/dotnet/sdk/blob/v10.0.401/src/Dotnet.Watch/Watch/HotReload/HotReloadDotNetWatcher.cs#L216) captures the local `evaluationResult` and stays subscribed to `fileWatcher.OnFileChange` ([L226](https://github.com/dotnet/sdk/blob/v10.0.401/src/Dotnet.Watch/Watch/HotReload/HotReloadDotNetWatcher.cs#L226)).
- When a change requires re-evaluation, [L393](https://github.com/dotnet/sdk/blob/v10.0.401/src/Dotnet.Watch/Watch/HotReload/HotReloadDotNetWatcher.cs#L393) assigns the result of `TryEvaluateProjectGraphAsync` to that local. When evaluation fails, it becomes `null`, and the loop waits for the next change with the callback still subscribed.
- On the next file event, the callback passes `null` to [`AcceptChange`](https://github.com/dotnet/sdk/blob/v10.0.401/src/Dotnet.Watch/Watch/HotReload/HotReloadDotNetWatcher.cs#L790), which reads `evaluationResult.Files`. The exception is thrown on a `FileSystemWatcher` thread pool callback, so it is unhandled and the process aborts.

The code is unchanged on `main`.

### Is this a regression?

Yes. It regressed in the 10.0.3xx feature band.

| SDK | Result (3 runs each) |
|---|---|
| 9.0.318 | No crash. `dotnet watch` reports the error and keeps running. |
| 10.0.100 | No crash. `dotnet watch` reports the error and keeps running. |
| 10.0.204 | No crash. `dotnet watch` reports the error and keeps running. |
| 10.0.300 | Crashes every time, same stack trace. |
| 10.0.401 | Crashes every time. |

Notes on the older runs:

- In every run that did not crash, the log shows the failed re-evaluation, `Fix the error to continue`, and then the delete event being processed normally.
- 9.0.318 and 10.0.100 print `Waiting for changes` only with `--verbose`, so the runs on older SDKs used `dotnet watch --verbose run` in the script.
- 9.0.318 re-evaluates through the `GenerateWatchList` target rather than a design-time compile, so for that run the marker target was also hooked `BeforeTargets="GenerateWatchList"`.

From the source: up to v10.0.204, a failed re-evaluation loops inside `EvaluateRootProjectAsync` until it succeeds, so `evaluationResult` is never `null`. From v10.0.300 on, `TryEvaluateProjectGraphAsync` returns `null` on failure and that is assigned to `evaluationResult`. That matches the runs above. The change came in #53466 (*Implements target framework selection for multi-targeted projects*).

### Are there any workarounds?

Avoid re-evaluation failures while `dotnet watch` runs. In our case, keeping the directory that gets rewritten out of what `dotnet watch` reacts to avoids it: adding `wwwroot/**` to `DefaultItemExcludes` only when `$(DotNetWatchBuild)` is `true`.

### dotnet --info output

```
.NET SDK:
 Version:           10.0.401
 Commit:            e34a38d2ae
 Workload version:  10.0.400-manifests.63b36e85
 MSBuild version:   18.9.11+e34a38d2a

Runtime Environment:
 OS Name:     Mac OS X
 OS Version:  26.7
 OS Platform: Darwin
 RID:         osx-arm64

Host:
  Version:      10.0.12
  Architecture: arm64
```

### IDE version

None: `dotnet watch run` from a terminal.

### Other details

Not tested on Linux or Windows; nothing in the cause is specific to macOS.

This issue was investigated and written up with an AI coding assistant (Claude Code).

Issues.Title: [release/3.1] Reset current_no_gc_region_info after leaving no gc region implicitly
Issues.Body:
Backport https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/73602.

## Customer Impact
Customers reported occasional `System.InvalidOperationException` with message `The NoGCRegion mode was already in progress` when calling `GC.TryStartNoGCRegion`. This is preventing them from using this optimization and impacting their cold start latencies.

## Testing
Customers have tried the fix on .NET 6 overnight and reported the exception never appears again. Meanwhile, there is an unpatched machine and observed 72 exceptions of the same type in the same time interval, proving this does fix the bug.

## Risk
Low. This only impact customer using `TryStartNoGCRegion`, and this is the right thing to do.

Issues.Title: Confusing behavior when using AssemblyInfo.cs
Issues.Body:
I'm completely perplexed.

I created a .Net Standard 2.0 library project.

I explicity added an AssemblyInfo.cs file, we need this because we use this utility to "stamp" our assemblies when we build them:

https://github.com/ygoe/NetRevisionTool

That utility is run as a pre/post build event and temporarily replaces placeholders in the AssemblyInformationalVersion attribute with runtime values (like repo folder name, commit ID, branch etc etc).

The completed assembly then has this info "burned" into it as we go forward.

This is just mind blowing, is there no way we can do this seemingly simple operation any more if adopt .Net Standard?

Issues.Title: Questions about tagging within this repository / future versions
Issues.Body:
I was looking through this repository to determine if .NET Standard 2.1 libraries support default interface methods - it looks like they do, given the presence of `System.Runtime.CompilerServices.RuntimeFeature.DefaultImplementationsOfInterfaces`, as well as my own experimenting in VS 2019. It seems I was mistaken when thinking that this was not the case, so I'm glad this repository is easily accessible to determine this.

But while doing this, I found it difficult to determine what commits were included in this particular .NET Standard version. I see that there's a tag `v2.1.0-prerelease.19126.1`, as well as branches `release/2.0.0`, `release/3.0`, and `release/3.0-preview9`. One of the machines I tested VS 2019 on had a `netstandard.dll` assembly, itself targeting .NETStandard v2.1.0, with AssemblyInformationalVersion `1.1.0+a5b5f2e1e369972c8ff1e2183979fab6099f52ef`; this commit is part of the `release/3.0` branch. However, another machine had a same-named assembly, targeting .NETCoreApp v3.0 and AssemblyInformationalVersion `3.0.0+4ac4c0367003fe3973a3648eb0715ddb0e3bbcea`, and I don't see that commit hash in this repository.

Additionally, [this blog post](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/dotnet/the-future-of-net-standard/) states that 2.1 will be the last version, but there is another prerelease tag `v2.2.0-prerelease.19564.1` and [on GitHub](https://github.com/dotnet/standard/releases/tag/v2.2.0-prerelease.19564.1) it's labelled .NET 5.0 Preview 2.

So I have a few questions for understanding this repository:

1. Since .NET Standard 2.1 is released, are there plans to continue development in this repository for e.g. the shared BCL going forward with .NET 5+?
2. Are there multiple kinds of `netstandard.dll` for a single .NET Standard version? E.g. are there separate versions for .NET Framework to reference and for .NET Core / .NET 5+ to reference?
3. Do the tags / branch names in this repository correspond to a .NET Standard version or something else?
4. It looks like there are patch releases; are there patch versions of a single .NET Standard version?
5. Are there other repositories which are being used to create `netstandard.dll`?
6. Is there a way to determine, from the repository, which commit is the one used for a given release?

Thank you for your consideration.
Issues.RelatedDescription: Closed issue "Questions about tagging within this repository / future versions" (#1777)

Issues.Title: Issue with resolving between .NET Standard 2.0 and .NET Standard 2.1
Issues.Body:
# Summary

.NET Standard version is not resolved correctly when a transitive dependency targets multiple .NET Standard versions.

# Environment

- Windows 10 (19042.746)
- .NET 5 SDK 5.0.201

# Minimal reproducible example
[bug.zip](https://github.com/dotnet/standard/files/6209239/bug.zip)

This is a three-project solution:
- `TestProject1` targeting `netcoreapp3.1`
- `ClassProject1` targeting `netstandard2.0`
- `ClassProject2` targeting *both* `netstandard2.0` and `netstandard2.1`

The project dependency chain is: `TestProject1 -> ClassProject1 -> ClassProject2`

A method (`ClassProject2Test1`) on `ClassProject2` is hidden behind a `#if NETSTANDARD2_0` preprocessor directive.

# The issue

The unit test failed with a `MissingMethodException`

```
[xUnit.net 00:00:00.38]     TestProject1.UnitTest1.Test1 [FAIL]
  Failed TestProject1.UnitTest1.Test1 [2 ms]
  Error Message:
   System.MissingMethodException : Method not found: 'Void ClassLibrary2.Class2.Class2Test1()'.
  Stack Trace:
     at ClassLibrary1.Class1.Class1Test1()
   at TestProject1.UnitTest1.Test1() in C:\Users\rex\source\netstandard-bug-repro\TestProject1\UnitTest1.cs:line 12
```

# Expected result

The compiler should have resolved the chain as:

`TestProject1 (.NET Core 3.1) -> ClassProject1 (.NET Standard 2.0) -> *ClassProject2 (.NET Standard 2.0)*` 

# Actual result

The compiler resolved the chain as:

`TestProject1 (.NET Core 3.1) -> ClassProject1 (.NET Standard 2.0) -> *ClassProject2 (.NET Standard 2.1)*` 

Which causes the exception because the offending method, `ClassProject2Test1`, was hidden by the `#if NETSTANDARD2_0` preprocessor directive.
Issues.RelatedDescription: Closed issue "Issue with resolving between .NET Standard 2.0 and .NET Standard 2.1" (#1787)

Issues.Title: Security Vulnerability due to System.Text.RegularExpressions
Issues.Body:
### Problem
There is a security vulnerability with the version of System.Text.RegularExpressions that is used by dotnet standard. The vulnerable version of System.Text.RegularExpressions is 4.3.0. Please see links below for the vulnerability documentation or discussion:

https://msrc.microsoft.com/update-guide/en-US/vulnerability/CVE-2019-0820
https://github.com/dotnet/announcements/issues/111
https://cve.mitre.org/cgi-bin/cvename.cgi?name=CVE-2019-0820
https://snyk.io/vuln/SNYK-DOTNET-SYSTEMTEXTREGULAREXPRESSIONS-174708
https://www.whitesourcesoftware.com/vulnerability-database/CVE-2019-0820

The dotnet commit that fixed the vulnerability is https://github.com/dotnet/corefx/commit/19d4b1163d8a03dd90ff5fd1785eea6305112545

### Issue:
We use whitesource and it has caught this issue with high severity. We don't consume System.Text.RegularExpressions directly but packages that use this. Therefore as a transitive dependency due to NetStandard library, which is being used by several other dotnet packages like Castle Windsor, MassTransit etc., Once an update is available the others could followup and update.

### Code:

[The latest version 2.0.3 of Net standard ](https://www.nuget.org/packages/NETStandard.Library/) still seem to be using System.Text.RegularExpressions version 4.3.0 as per https://github.com/dotnet/standard/blob/master/src/apicompat/netstandard/netstandard.depproj

### Fix
Please update[ library](https://www.nuget.org/packages/NETStandard.Library/) targeting .netStandard 1.6 to update System.Text.RegularExpression package to latest secured version 4.3.1 to fix the security issue or kindly suggest alternatives.
Issues.RelatedDescription: Closed issue "Security Vulnerability due to System.Text.RegularExpressions" (#1786)

Issues.Title: linq using GetValueOrDefault  in Where clause problem
Issues.Body:
Hello,

I am currently using .NET core 2.2.x and EF Core. 2.2.6. I have a function that returns a List<Animal> from the database with no issue. It returns 11 results. However, when I try to use `.Where(p => p.DeletedAt.GetValueOrDefault(DateTime.Now) => DateTime.Now).ToList()`, it still should return 11 results, however it returns 0. I also eliminated the possibility that there is something wrong with my where clause (logic) because it works perfectly on 4.6.1 EF Core 2.2.6. Furthermore, I confirmed that it is only where I am comparing a nullable type using that function and I am guessing that I missed a thread someone opened on this issue. I am aware .NET core 2.2 is not LTS. I also thought this goes here because it's not AFAIK, an EF core issue but rather an Ienumerable/Linq issue.

Update: As it turns out your notion of `DateTime.Now` getting evaluated twice is true. To rectify that, I will now be using `DateTime.Now.Date`. This is odd because this exact code works on 4.6.1. You're probably right. SMH. Thank you @GrabYourPitchforks! You may now close.
Issues.RelatedDescription: Closed issue "linq using GetValueOrDefault  in Where clause problem" (#1792)

Issues.Title: Strong name signature not valid
Issues.Body:
Since I've ported a ClickOnce application from .NET Framework 4.6.1 to .NET Standard 2.0, the message _"Strong assembly name signature not valid for **Microsoft.SqlServer.Assessment.Types.dll**"_ appears when trying to install or update the application. So the next step was to verify the assembly strong name by using the [Strong Name Tool](https://docs.microsoft.com/dotnet/framework/tools/sn-exe-strong-name-tool) to make sure, that everything is fine, but:

```sh
> sn.exe -v Microsoft.SqlServer.Assessment.Types.dll

Microsoft (R) .NET Framework Strong Name Utility Version 4.0.30319.0
Copyright (c) Microsoft Corporation. All rights reserved.

Microsoft.SqlServer.Assessment.Types.dll is a delay-signed or test-signed assembly
```

Additional information:

- The assembly versions `161.46041.41` and `161.46367.54` ended up in the same result
- This issue looks very similar to [this](https://www.damirscorner.com/blog/posts/20140502-StrongNameValidationFailedSecurityException.html)
- @markingmyname / @olprod: The root package, which is required for [Server Management Objects (SMOs)](https://docs.microsoft.com/sql/relational-databases/server-management-objects-smo/overview-smo?view=sql-server-ver15), is:
  - [Microsoft.SqlServer.SqlManagementObjects](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Microsoft.SqlServer.SqlManagementObjects)
    - Microsoft.SqlServer.Assessment
      - Microsoft.SqlServer.Assessment.Authoring
        - **Microsoft.SqlServer.Assessment.Types.dll**
- This issue appears on windows server machines but the software runs on different machines and I would like to avoid temporary workarounds such as editing the registry and activate the strong name bypass feature because of the forced validation on windows server machines
Issues.RelatedDescription: Closed issue "Strong name signature not valid" (#1789)

Issues.Title: System.Drawing.Printing.PrinterSettings slow
Issues.Body:
_This issue has been moved from [a ticket on Developer Community](https://developercommunity2.visualstudio.com/t/SystemDrawingPrintingPrinterSettings-/890524)._ --- Hello I'm debugging a problem with the printer settings. Some calls are significant slower if the default printer is a network printer, even if I explicit set a local printer name. After studying referencesource I think I found the culprit. I call: var printerSettings = new System.Drawing.Printing.PrinterSettings(); printerSettings.PrinterName = "LOCALPRINTER"; // the next call is slow if the OS default printer is a network printer var res = printerSettings.DefaultPageSettings.PrinterResolution Internally FastDeviceCapabilities is called. FastDeviceCapabilities calls GetOutputPort. But GetOutput port return the port of the default printer and not the port of the given printer! In addition, DeviceCapabilities is then called with a wrong combination of printer name and port, don't know if this could lead to additional problems. Resolution: GetOutputPort should return the port of the given printer and not accessing the default printer at all. Best Regards, Raphael --- ### Original Comments #### Raphael Affolter on 1/20/2020, 04:03 AM:

I forgot to mention: .Net Framework 4.6.1

#### Feedback Bot on 1/20/2020, 06:51 PM:

We have directed your feedback to the appropriate engineering team for further evaluation. The team will review the feedback and notify you about the next steps.

#### Raphael Affolter on 2/7/2020, 08:39 AM:

Because we print a lot, we really suffer from this performance penalty.

Also reading PaperSizes and PaperSources from the printer settings is slow caused by the same problem.

Could you please inform me about a possible fix?

Best Regards,

Raphael

#### Raphael Affolter on 2/7/2020, 10:33 AM:

In my opinion the fix is easy: replace GetOutputPort by OutputPort in the call to

FastDeviceCapabilities.

Done.

Issues.Title: Build issues when referencing project that targets multiple frameworks C# WPF
Issues.Body:
I'm working on converting a large WPF solution's projects to SDK style and ran into some issues.

The solution is large with multiple projects(old style) all targeting .net452 and some nugets(some made by me) installed, targeting both .net452 and .netstandard2.1 This all seems to work fine, somehow the nuget manages to install the correct version targeting .net452.

I have decided to slowly convert the projects inside the solution to SDK style targeting .net452 and .netstandard2.1 just like the nugets.

This is where the problem starts, one project was converted so far that is referenced by multiple other projects. Localy everything seems to build and run fine, however when Azure DevOps(VS version 2019) is used to build the solution there are 2 scenarios:

1. The famous error message is shown:

                "Error CS0012: The type 'Object' is defined in an assembly that is not referenced. You must add a reference to assembly 
                 'netstandard, Version=2.1.0.0"

2. It builds fine but on app launch it crashes with:

                 "Could not load file or assembly 'netstandard, Version=2.1.0.0, Culture=neutral, PublicKeyToken=cc7b13ffcd2ddd51' 
                 or one of its dependencies. The system cannot find the file specified."

I'm suspecting that the problem is related to referencing the SDK project, it looks like that somehow it references the .netstandard2.1 instead of the .net452.

The reason this is my suspicion is that if targetframework is set to only .net452 on the referenced project everything works fine. Google has led me to two possible solutions to tell the project what framework to use from the reference:

```
<ProjectReference Include="..\..\..\..\foo\foo.csproj"
                  AdditionalProperties="TargetFramework=net452">
      <Project>{xxxxxx-xxxxxx-xxxxx-xxxxx-xxxxxxx}</Project>
      <Name>foo</Name>
</ProjectReference>
```
and

```
<ProjectReference Include="..\..\..\..\foo\foo.csproj">
      <SetTargetFramework>TargetFramework=net452</SetTargetFramework>
      <Project>{xxxxxx-xxxxxx-xxxxx-xxxxx-xxxxxxx}</Project>
      <<Name>foo</Name>
</ProjectReference>
```
This doesn't look like it's doing anything and the problem still persists. At the moment I ran out of ideas and I'm here asking for help. Please let me know what I'm doing wrong or what else I can try.
Issues.RelatedDescription: Closed issue "Build issues when referencing project that targets multiple frameworks C# WPF" (#1776)

Issues.Title: Migrate FabricBot Tasks to Config-as-Code
Issues.Body:
**TL;DR;** Requesting to add [FabricBot](https://eng.ms/docs/products/1es-data-insights/merlinbot/extensions/fabricbot_overview) configuration associated with your repository to `.github/fabricbot.json`.

**Context**

FabricBot is now a [config-as-code-only](https://eng.ms/docs/products/1es-data-insights/merlinbot/extensions/bot-config-as-code) platform. As a result, while you can still use the [FabricBot Configuration Portal](https://portal.fabricbot.ms/bot/?repo=dotnet/corefx) to modify your FabricBot configuration, you can no longer save the changes. The only way to save changes to your configuration at the moment is to _export configuration_ from the portal and upload the exported configuration to `.github/fabricbot.json` in your repository. In this pull request, we are adding your FabricBot configuration to your repository at `.github/fabricbot.json` so that you can make changes to it going forward.

While the [FabricBot Configuration Portal](https://portal.fabricbot.ms/bot/?repo=dotnet/corefx) is the *only way* to modify your FabricBot configuration at the moment, we have a feature on our backlog to publish the JSON schema defining the structure of the FabricBot configuration file. Issues.Title: Fix RSA OAEP decryption in OpenSSL with non-power-of-two keys lengths
Issues.Body:
## Customer Impact

A customer reported in dotnet/runtime#71607 that decrypting RSA OAEP with SHA2 and a 3072-bit key on Linux resulted in a OAEP de-padding error, while other platforms were able to perform these operations successfully.

Investigation in to the issue led to uncover that RSA OAEP decryption that uses the managed implementation does not work with non-power-of-two keys because we do not slice a rented buffer accordingly. The current implementation only works because `CryptoPool.Rent` happens to give back power-of-two arrays which are exactly the same size as the key.

The fix is to slice the data to the correct size.

This does not affect dotnet/runtime because the managed implementation of RSA OAEP is no longer used for OpenSSL RSA decryption. This change was introduced in dotnet/runtime#50063.

## Testing

Unit tests were introduced to test RSA OAEP encryption with a 3072-bit RSA key. These tests will be forward-ported to dotnet/runtime.

## Risk

Minimal. The change is localized and understood that a `Slice` was missing.

Issues.Title: Format Hover
Issues.Body:
# Format Hover

## Motivation

It's often useful when writing C# format strings to understand what they mean. Documentation for the supported formats is available on Microsoft Learn. This PR extracts that information and attaches it to known framework types that support formatting.

There are multiple pieces of this with increasing complexity.

First we can identify the general format.

![Format description and Microsoft Learn link](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sharifhsn/roslyn/b9814c9fdfc22fc62d3875b8001013c120137804/format-description.jpg)

When possible, we can generate a preview of what the formatted value would look like. This is done for compiler constants as well as when we can infer a local variable's value and rule out mutation, capture, or reference aliasing:

![Preview of an inferred local value](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sharifhsn/roslyn/b9814c9fdfc22fc62d3875b8001013c120137804/value-preview.jpg)

No project code is executed. Previews use an explicit supported culture when it can be resolved, and en-US otherwise.

This can also be displayed through an opt-in inlay hint.

![Opt-in format preview inlay hints](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sharifhsn/roslyn/b9814c9fdfc22fc62d3875b8001013c120137804/inlay-hints.jpg)

When the input cannot be statically verified or does not have a known value, the PR can use fixed samples to demonstrate the format.

![Fixed sample under the Example heading](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sharifhsn/roslyn/b9814c9fdfc22fc62d3875b8001013c120137804/fallback-example.jpg)

This supports many different types.

![Examples across supported framework types](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sharifhsn/roslyn/b9814c9fdfc22fc62d3875b8001013c120137804/supported-types.jpg)

### References

- [Earlier Roslyn request for embedded-language tooltips](https://github.com/dotnet/roslyn/issues/65531), closed as not planned.
- [Roslyn's existing date/time format completion](https://github.com/dotnet/roslyn/blob/38bc4bcb0612b786aa8bded52768c7133fde0ab5/src/Features/Core/Portable/EmbeddedLanguages/DateAndTime/DateAndTimeEmbeddedCompletionProvider.cs).
- [ReSharper format-specifier completion, descriptions, and previews](https://blog.jetbrains.com/dotnet/2013/07/02/code-completion-improvements-in-resharper-8/).
- [RoslynSense format-component hover and examples](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=GerardSmit.roslyn-sense).
- [Roslyn's LSP inlay-hint implementation](https://github.com/dotnet/roslyn/pull/67319).
- [Microsoft Learn: formatting types in .NET](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/base-types/formatting-types).

Issues.Title: Specify that ProjectData tasks are .NET
Issues.Body:
These tasks are built only for modern .NET, so if they're triggered in
an MSBuild.exe-hosted build, they emit a warning

    MSBUILD : warning : The custom task 'Microsoft.NET.ProjectData.Tasks' required a fallback to out-of-process execution because the UsingTask definition does not specify the correct Runtime and Architecture. This reduces build performance. Update the UsingTask element to explicitly specify Runtime and Architecture attributes (e.g., Runtime="CLR4" Architecture="x64") or use TaskFactory="TaskHostFactory".

That's because MSBuild detects the target framework of the DLL and runs
it compatibly--but the warning is annoying. Specifying that the task
run in a modern .NET TaskHost codifies that behavior without the perf
hit of failing to load the task, analyzing why, and retrying in the
right process.

Issues.Title: File-based apps: go-to-definition for `#:include`, `#:project`, and `#:ref` directives
Issues.Body:
Replacement for #84756 which got stale.

This now uses just the workspaces Project representation to find navigation targets, and the file-based apps helpers to interpret the directives.

`#:include Files/**/*.cs` and similar globs are supported. Multiple navigation targets are returned where applicable.

Following cases are not supported:
- `#:include MyFile?.cs`. `?` apparently is a pattern matching a single character. It works in msbuild but is not supported by the globbing library, at least not the way I am using it, and seems uncommon/unimportant.
- `#:include $(MyProperty)/File.cs`. This also seems uncommon in practice but we could consider a future improvement to have the project system expand these before trying to navigate.
- `#:include File1.cs;File2.cs`. Also uncommon.

This adds a package reference to workspaces layer, so I created a test insertion: https://dev.azure.com/devdiv/DevDiv/_git/VS/pullrequest/803246

This feature is not expected to work in VS, so, no new DLL loads are expected in VS. But the insertion should help us verify that the new package reference doesn't break product construction or deployment.

Issues.Title: Blazor event debounce and throttling prototype
Issues.Body:
## Summary

This PR is the Razor compiler half of a prototype for Blazor event debouncing and throttling (https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/10522), paired with the runtime change in https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/70311.

## Architecture

The implementation extends the existing `@on{EVENT}:preventDefault` and `@on{EVENT}:stopPropagation` directive attribute parameter pipeline:

1. **Tag helper production (`EventHandlerTagHelperProducer`):** Following the existing `preventDefault` and `stopPropagation` rules, `EventHandlerTagHelperProducer` registers `:debounce` and `:throttle` (`int` milliseconds) tag matching rules and `BoundAttributeParameter` descriptors on event handler tag helpers, and stores the `[EventHandler]` attribute's `EventThrottleMode` in `EventHandlerMetadata`.
2. **IR lowering and code generation (`ComponentEventHandlerLoweringPass` & `ComponentNodeWriter`):** Just as `preventDefault` and `stopPropagation` lower to `ComponentAttributeIntermediateNode` calls to `AddEventPreventDefaultAttribute` and `AddEventStopPropagationAttribute`, `:debounce` and `:throttle` lower to `AddEventDebounceAttribute` and `AddEventThrottleAttribute` (appending `EventThrottleMode.LeadingAndTrailing` when specified in `EventHandlerMetadata`). Because `ComponentEventHandlerLoweringPass` runs before `ComponentBindLoweringPass`, `@bind` with `@bind:event="oninput"` and `@oninput:debounce="300"` works automatically.
3. **Diagnostics (`ComponentDiagnosticFactory`):** Following the existing duplicate and mutually exclusive `@bind` parameter diagnostics (such as `RZ10018`), the pass reports `RZ10031` when `:debounce` and `:throttle` are combined on the same event and `RZ10032` when used as a minimized attribute without an interval value.

Issues.Title: Fix nullable annotation warning from nameof emission for a generic component parameter
Issues.Body:
Fixes dotnet/aspnetcore#69947.

Using a generic component with a nullable type argument together with another parameter:

```razor
<MyComponent T="string?" Param="1" />
```

makes the compiler emit the parameter name as `nameof(global::...MyComponent<string?>.Param)`. In `WriteComponentAttributeName` the property name goes through a source-mapped pragma, which carries `#nullable restore`, but the containing type is written raw, so `string?` lands in a `#nullable disable` region and the caller's generated code warns CS8669.

This change writes the containing type between `#nullable restore` and `#nullable disable` when its text contains a nullable annotation and nullability enforcement is not suppressed, following the pattern `InjectTargetExtension` already uses for `@inject`. Types without an annotation emit exactly as before.

Tests: adds `AddComponentParameter_WithNameof_GenericComponent_NullableTypeArgument` with baselines. The full `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Razor.Language` test project passes with no other baseline changes: 4,649 passed, 0 failed, on both net10.0 and net472.

Related: dotnet/roslyn#85648 reports the same warning through `@bind`. This change covers the `AddComponentParameter` nameof path; I haven't verified it against the `@bind` scenario.

Issues.Title: Terminate multiline C# attribute values when formatting Razor
Issues.Body:
Fixes #86306 (the bound case described in [this comment](https://github.com/dotnet/roslyn/issues/86306#issuecomment-6632823628)).

In `VisitMultilineCSharpExpressionLiteral`, the last line of a multiline expression only got a `;` for block-bodied lambdas. A C# expression that is the whole value of a component or directive attribute was left unterminated:

```razor
<button @onclick="() => Show(1,
                  2)"
   class="x">y</button>
```

Roslyn then read the next attribute line as part of the expression, and `class="x"` landed one level too shallow in every attribute indent style. The `@onclick="@(() => …)"` form was already right. This extends the `emitSemiColon` condition to `node.Parent is MarkupTagHelperAttributeValueSyntax`, still only when the line continues past the expression.

Tests:
- New in `RazorFormatterTest`: `TryFormatAsync_MultilineDirectiveAttributeLambda`, plus `_IndentByOne` and `_IndentByTwo`.
- New in `DocumentFormattingTest`: `MultilineLambdaInDirectiveAttribute_MovesWithTag`, plus `_IndentByOne` and `_IndentByTwo`.
- The expected output for each test is what the `@(` form produces on `main`. Without the new condition, all 6 fail.
- `Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.Razor.DotNetFormat.UnitTests` passes, 35 of 35.
- The cohosting formatting tests pass, 652 passed and 1 skipped, including the multiline lambda tests from #84121.

Not verified: the hand-written `htmlFormatted` values against WebTools, which only runs on .NET Framework, and the net472 VS test project.

Issues.Title: Close Html elements whose end tag isn't first on a line in Razor formatting
Issues.Body: Fixes #86304 `CSharpDocumentGenerator` turns an element that causes indentation into a `{` (in `VisitStartTag`) and its end tag into a `}` (in `VisitEndTag`). But `Generate()` only visits the first node on each line, so an end tag later in a line never emitted its `}`. Everything after it was indented one level too deep, to the end of the file. A Razor comment in front of the end tag is one way to get there. `text `, `a `, `@DateTime.Now ` and ` ` all fail the same way. The fix: - **Track the open braces:** the generator records the positions of start tags it emitted `{` for. - **Emit the missing braces:** after visiting a line, it emits a `}` for each later end tag in that line whose start tag is in that set. The braces go on lines after the current one, which keeps the line indented as content of the element. Those lines are then skipped when mapping back. - **Skip by count:** the C# formatter splits `}}` onto separate lines, so `LineInfo.SkipNextLine` (bool) becomes `SkipNextLines` (int). The generator is shared, so the cohosted path has the same bug whenever the Html formatter leaves the end tag on that line. `DocumentFormattingTest.EndTagAfterRazorCommentOnSameLine` covers it. Tests: - New: `RazorFormatterTest.TryFormatAsync_EndTagAfterRazorCommentOnSameLine`, `TryFormatAsync_MultipleEndTagsAfterRazorCommentOnSameLine` (`@* note *@ `), and `DocumentFormattingTest.EndTagAfterRazorCommentOnSameLine`. - Without the new call, all three fail. With `iFormatted++` instead of `+= SkipNextLines`, the multiple-end-tags test fails. - `Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.Razor.DotNetFormat.UnitTests` passes, 34 of 34. - The cohosting formatting tests pass, 650 passed and 1 skipped. They were run through `Microsoft.VisualStudioCode.RazorExtension.UnitTests` on macOS. Two things I couldn't check. The cohost test passes `validateHtmlFormattedMatchesWebTools: false` (that check only runs on .NET Framework), and I haven't run the net472-only VS test project. Not covered here: a start tag later in a line (`text ` … ``) has the mirror-image problem for its contents. Seen in the wild in dotnet/eShop `src/HybridApp/Components/Layout/HeaderBar.razor`. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) ###### Microsoft Reviewers: [Open in CodeFlow](https://microsoft.github.io/open-pr/?codeflow=https://github.com/dotnet/roslyn/pull/86308)

Issues.Title: Indent Razor by indent_size under dotnet format
Issues.Body:
Fixes #86303

The formatting engine indents by `FormattingEngineOptions.TabSize` columns per level, as an LSP client's `tabSize`. The `dotnet format` entry point (`RazorFormatter.GetFormattingOptions`) filled it from `tab_width`, so `indent_size` was ignored. With `indent_size = 2` and `tab_width = 4`, both the markup and the C# in `@code` blocks were indented by 4. `GetResolvedCSharpSyntaxFormattingOptions` sets `IndentationSize` from the same value.

With spaces, this passes `indent_size`. With tabs, a level is one tab, so it keeps `tab_width`. That matters for how aligned columns are written: `TryFormatAsync_IndentsByTabsUsingOneTabPerLevel` aligns an attribute, and passing `indent_size` there would write four tabs where two tabs and two spaces are right at `tab_width = 4`.

Only the `dotnet format` entry point changes; the cohosted path still takes `tabSize` from the client.

Tests: the two new tests in `RazorFormatterTest`. The spaces test fails without the fix, and the tabs test fails with the simpler `TabSize = IndentationSize`. `Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.Razor.DotNetFormat.UnitTests` passes, 34 of 34.

I found this while comparing a Razor formatter of my own against this one through the `Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.Razor.DotNetFormat` package.

``` The continuation line is re-indented, which changes the attribute's value. That's harmless for `class`, but not for `title`, `alt`, `value`, `placeholder` or `data-*`.

Issues.Title: Razor formatting (dotnet format) indents markup by tab_width and ignores indent_size
Issues.Body:
### Version Used `main` at 535114b10a6, and the `Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.Razor.DotNetFormat` 11.2.0-preview.26553.101 package. Reproduced through `RazorFormatter.TryFormatAsync`, the entry point `dotnet format` uses. ### Steps to Reproduce `.editorconfig`: ```ini root = true [*] indent_style = space indent_size = 2 tab_width = 4 ``` A `.razor` file already indented by 2: ```razor

x

``` ### Expected Behavior Unchanged. `indent_size` is the width of one indentation level, and `tab_width` is how wide a tab character is displayed. ### Actual Behavior Markup is re-indented by `tab_width` columns per level: ```razor

x

``` `indent_size` has no effect. The C# formatter honours `indent_size`, so under the same settings a `.razor` file's C# and markup end up indented differently. The cause looks to be `RazorFormatter.GetFormattingOptions` in `Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.Razor.DotNetFormat`. It sets `FormattingEngineOptions.TabSize`, which the engine uses as the indentation unit (like LSP's `tabSize`), from `LineFormatting.TabSize` rather than `LineFormatting.IndentationSize`. Related: #85310, the general `.editorconfig` tracking issue. This one is specific to the `dotnet format` entry point, which already reads `.editorconfig`.

Issues.Title: Migrate ContainedLanguage to the generated protocol assembly
Issues.Body:
Migrate the existing net472 ContainedLanguage path to `Microsoft.VisualStudio.LanguageServer.Protocol.Internal` 18.14.8 and remove references, VSIX deployment entries, and codebase registrations for the old `Protocol` and `Protocol.Extensions` assemblies.

Upgrade `Client` and `Client.Implementation` together to 18.14.30 so the implementation package no longer restores the frozen protocol graph. Raise the existing shared editor package floor to 18.13.5 and internal interop/shell floors to 18.11.573, as required by those dependencies and central transitive pinning. Framework conditions and API-check settings are unchanged; there are no unrelated Roslyn LSP model rewrites.

**Binary compatibility:** `FormattingOptionsProvider.GetOptions(Uri)` now returns `FormattingOptions` from `Microsoft.VisualStudio.LanguageServer.Protocol.Internal, Version=18.14.8.0`, rather than the old `Microsoft.VisualStudio.LanguageServer.Protocol` assembly. The namespace and textual API signature are unchanged, but the assembly-qualified return type is not binary-compatible. Downstream callers and implementations using that API must be rebuilt; an assembly-version binding redirect does not bridge the different assembly names. The generic request-invocation and document/virtual-document APIs are unchanged.

**Release order:** Internal 18.14.8 and Client/Implementation 18.14.30 were published from producer commit `f72be3306748a6c07a74366c1a774def4bb0fb19` and are available through the normal vs-impl/vssdk feeds. After this change lands, an official build must publish the migrated ContainedLanguage package and its normal Roslyn package dependencies before downstream consumers can select the resulting real package version and rebuild. This draft does not publish packages or assume a future ContainedLanguage version.

Published Internal 18.14.8 incorporates [merged protocol support PR 803304](https://dev.azure.com/devdiv/DevDiv/_git/VSLanguageServerClient/pullrequest/803304): public `ProtocolJsonSerializerOptions.Configure` and a single netstandard2.0 asset instead of net472. ContainedLanguage itself remains net472. Matching VS runtime integration is tracked by [VS insertion PR 803509](https://devdiv.visualstudio.com/DevDiv/_git/VS/pullrequest/803509?_a=overview); its current merge state and matching installed-runtime availability remain unverified. Published packages and a successful insertion task do not establish that the matching runtime is integrated or installed.

Issues.Title: Support roslyn-language-server tool installation on FreeBSD
Issues.Body:
### Problem

The new `roslyn-language-server` .NET tool cannot currently be installed with the stable FreeBSD SDK. On FreeBSD 15.1 amd64 with the native FreeBSD Ports SDK 9.0.115/runtime 9.0.14 (`RID: freebsd.15-x64`):

```text
$ dotnet tool install roslyn-language-server --prerelease --tool-path ./roslyn-tool
The settings file in the tool's NuGet package is invalid: Format version is higher than supported.
This tool may not be supported in this SDK version. Update your SDK.
```

Roslyn main now requires .NET 10 and `LanguageServerPublish.props` publishes apphosts only for Windows, Linux, Linux-musl and macOS RIDs. FreeBSD Ports currently packages stable .NET 9/8; `lang/dotnet-devel` is an unpackaged .NET 10 alpha bootstrap port.

### Existing native evidence

This is not a request based only on package metadata. Using native FreeBSD .NET 9 and the platform-neutral managed Roslyn 4.14.0 language-server payload, we validated on FreeBSD 15.1 amd64:

- C# console build and execution
- LSP initialize
- completion and diagnostics in Code - OSS
- hover and go-to-definition
- rename returning the expected edits

The downstream integration and exact limitations are recorded in [EriduOs PR #12](https://github.com/tomblanchard312/EriduOs/pull/12).

### Suggested direction

Once a supported FreeBSD .NET 10 SDK/runtime is available, could the tool packaging either:

1. publish `freebsd-x64`/`freebsd-arm64` framework-dependent assets, or
2. include a portable managed fallback that launches `Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.LanguageServer.dll` through the current `dotnet` host when no platform apphost is packaged?

I can prepare and test the Roslyn-side change against native FreeBSD once the .NET 10 prerequisite is available. I did not add FreeBSD RIDs blindly because the current official build cannot restore/test the corresponding .NET 10 host packs, and doing so would create an unverified package.
Issues.RelatedDescription: Open issue "Support roslyn-language-server tool installation on FreeBSD" (#86296)

Issues.Title: dotnetup: enumerate system installs without loading hostfxr
Issues.Body:
Fixes https://github.com/dotnet/sdk/issues/56932

## Summary

Replace dotnetup's hostfxr-based system install discovery with a small on-disk enumerator, and delete the now-unused `HostFxrWrapper`.

- Walk `sdk/<version>` and `shared/<framework>/<version>` using one marker-file helper shared with `InstallationValidator`: `dotnet.dll` for SDKs and `<framework>.deps.json` for runtimes. Ignore invalid version names and folders without the appropriate marker.
- Do not load native libraries, set `HOSTFXR_PATH`, or require a muxer or `host/fxr` directory for discovery. Valid component folders in partial roots are now discoverable.
- Preserve system-root discovery, current-process architecture tagging/filtering, unknown-framework mapping, root-priority deduplication, descending version ordering, and on-disk folder versions. This does not introduce multilevel lookup or change `.version` interpretation.
- Retain per-root filesystem-failure warnings and telemetry, now named `system_install.enumeration_*` instead of `hostfxr.enumeration_*`.
- Update the two design references that described the removed hostfxr path.

Installation validation keeps its existing muxer requirements and Windows Desktop exception; only the component-marker check is shared. Architecture detection of the actual root is intentionally unchanged.

## Validation

- Focused `SystemInstallEnumeratorTests`, `InstallationValidatorTests`, and `InitWorkflowTests`: **44 passed, 2 non-Windows-only tests skipped**, no failures.
- Regression coverage includes missing and invalid hostfxr, all supported component markers, invalid versions, incorrect framework markers, unknown frameworks, missing/empty roots, folder-version preservation, and root-priority/version ordering.
- Built dotnetup, including its **Windows x64 NativeAOT publish**, with **0 warnings and 0 errors**.
- Changed-file formatting verification, `git diff --check`, and local Markdown link/anchor validation passed.

Tests were run through `scripts/RunTests.cs` with isolated artifacts. Validation was local on Windows; cross-platform execution is left to CI.
Issues.RelatedDescription: Open PR "dotnetup: enumerate system installs without loading hostfxr" (#56935)

But it helps automatically click and progress the installer forward. With /quiet, the window requires user interaction to proceed but this automates away some of that.

Issues.Title: Avoid no-op CI investigator environment stalls and oversized job outputs
Issues.Body:
## Summary

The CI Investigator stopped filing issues, seemingly because of a GitHub incident:
https://www.githubstatus.com/incidents/dqn46wtvbdzv
https://www.githubstatus.com/incidents/djlmxz2zd0j7

In this incident, actions workflows had a 'loss of run state' bug, which causes jobs to permanently block and never proceed past 'pre-activation'. That's exactly what happened with our workflow, and it is within the specified outage windows:

The problematic run was:  https://github.com/dotnet/sdk/actions/runs/37442110088

This PR fixes two issues to try to reduce the potential for this problem given any future outage:
- GitHub's 1 MB job-output channel blocked sending 'evidence' including failed test results for large failure outputs, which prevented the investigator from running. 

- Empty/skipped runs used to request the protected PAT environment, which was wasteful and could block the queue unnecessarily.

- The workflow-wide concurrency lock let one stuck run block every later investigation. Only the `collect` job (which owns the processed-build checkpoint) is now serialized; other jobs run per-run, so a stuck admission blocks only its own run. Issues now record failure and mechanism fingerprints for cross-run deduplication; rare duplicates are possible when two runs investigate the same failure concurrently.

- gh-aw v0.89 stopped exporting the safe-output temporary ID map, so a run that filed several issues dispatched Issue Monster only for the first. The dispatcher now also finds this run's open `live-build-incident` issues by gh-aw's provenance marker. Verified e2e in the fork: https://github.com/nagilson/sdk/actions/runs/41937928505 filed 3 issues and dispatched Issue Monster for all 3.

Alternatives:
- We could make a pipeline that clears out the queue, though I avoided doing so because it seems like hacky extra cost to workaround a GH infra issue.
Issues.RelatedDescription: Open PR "Avoid no-op CI investigator environment stalls and oversized job outputs" (#56934)

Issues.Title: dotnetup: enumerate system installs with the folder rules instead of loading hostfxr
Issues.Body:
Follow-up from https://github.com/dotnet/sdk/pull/56913.

## Problem

`DotnetEnvironmentManager.GetExistingSystemInstalls` lists the SDKs and runtimes in each system install root by calling `HostFxrWrapper.getInstalls`, which loads the root's native hostfxr into the dotnetup process and calls `hostfxr_get_dotnet_environment_info`.

- [DotnetEnvironmentManager.cs](https://github.com/dotnet/sdk/blob/release/dnup/src/Installer/dotnetup.Library/DotnetEnvironmentManager.cs) (`GetExistingSystemInstalls`)
- [HostFxrWrapper.cs](https://github.com/dotnet/sdk/blob/release/dnup/src/Installer/Microsoft.Dotnet.Installation/Internal/HostFxrWrapper.cs) (`getInstalls`, `PreloadHostFxrLibrary`)

This has costs:

- **Native loading can fail.** It throws when `host/fxr` is missing or the loaded hostfxr doesn't export `hostfxr_get_dotnet_environment_info`. The failure is reported as a warning and the root is skipped.
- **Process-wide state.** On Unix, `PreloadHostFxrLibrary` sets `HOSTFXR_PATH` with `AppContext.SetData`, which carries over to later roots in the same process. On Windows, the first hostfxr loaded may serve every later call.
- **Two definitions of an install.** `InstallationValidator` already copies the host's rules for what counts as an install: an SDK folder with `dotnet.dll`, a framework folder with `<framework>.deps.json`. Listing system installs uses hostfxr instead, so the two can disagree.

## Proposal

Enumerate `sdk/*` and `shared/<framework>/*` under each system root with the same rules `InstallationValidator` uses, and remove the hostfxr dependency from this path. Keep one shared helper for "is this folder an install" so validation and listing can't drift apart.

## To check

- Whether anything else relies on hostfxr's view, such as how it treats multilevel lookup or install locations.
- Behavior when a root has no `host/fxr` (a partial install), which works with a folder walk but fails today.
- Architecture handling: `getInstalls` stamps every install with the current process architecture.

## Notes

- System installs report the on-disk folder version as `Version`. For RTM and servicing daily builds that differs from the build version, and `.version` can't recover it for runtimes. SDK `.version` line 4 holds the full build version even for stable releases (for example `10.0.403-servicing.26523.112`). This issue doesn't need to change that.
Issues.RelatedDescription: Open issue "dotnetup: enumerate system installs with the folder rules instead of loading hostfxr" (#56932)

Issues.Title: Every dotnet command waits 2 s on SDK 11 RC2/RC3 (Linux): the telemetry exporter's Azure VM metadata request to 169.254.169.254 times out
Issues.Body:
## Summary

On Linux, every `dotnet` command under SDK 11.0.100 RC2 and RC3 takes about 2 seconds longer than it should, including `dotnet --version`. The CLI telemetry exporter requests Azure VM metadata from `169.254.169.254` and waits for that request to time out before the process exits. On a machine that isn't an Azure VM, that address is routed through the default gateway, which silently drops it, so every command pays the full timeout.

SDK 10.0.402 on the same machine is not affected. Setting `DOTNET_CLI_TELEMETRY_OPTOUT=1` removes the delay.

## Environment

- Ubuntu 26.04.1 LTS, x64 (`linux-x64`)
- SDK `11.0.100-rc.3.26522.148` and `11.0.100-rc.2.26504.105`, compared with `10.0.402`, each selected with a `global.json` pin
- No `OTEL_*`, `APPLICATIONINSIGHTS_*` or `DOTNET_CLI_TELEMETRY_*` variables set except where the table says so
- An ordinary home network: `ip route get 169.254.169.254` resolves through the default gateway; there's no link-local route

## Reproduction

```sh
time dotnet --version
```

| Configuration | Wall time |
|---|---|
| SDK 10.0.402, default | 0.06 s |
| SDK 11.0.100-rc.2.26504.105, default | 2.02 s |
| SDK 11.0.100-rc.3.26522.148, default | 2.02 s |
| RC3, `DOTNET_CLI_TELEMETRY_OPTOUT=1` | 0.01 s |
| RC3, `DOTNET_CLI_TELEMETRY_SHUTDOWN_TIMEOUT_MS=0`, `100` or `500` | 2.02 s |
| RC3, `APPLICATIONINSIGHTS_STATSBEAT_DISABLED=true` | 2.02 s |
| RC3, telemetry on, connections to `169.254.169.254` refused immediately (`LD_PRELOAD` shim on `connect`) | 0.02 s |

The time is spent waiting, not computing: `real 2.03s`, `user 0.03s`.

## What the trace shows

`strace -f -tt -e trace=connect,sendto,exit_group dotnet --version` with RC3, times relative to the first connection:

- +0.00 s: `connect` to `::ffff:169.254.169.254` port 80 returns `EINPROGRESS` and never completes.
- +0.05 s: `connect` to the Application Insights ingestion endpoint on port 443; the TLS handshake completes and the telemetry payload is sent by +0.68 s.
- +0.87 s: a second `connect` to `::ffff:169.254.169.254` port 80.
- +2.00 s: `exit_group(0)`.

The process exits 2.00 s after the first metadata request, long after the telemetry upload has finished.

The address appears in the SDK's `Azure.Monitor.OpenTelemetry.Exporter.dll` as `http://169.254.169.254/metadata/instance/compute?api-version=2017-08-01&format=json`. The SDK's `Microsoft.Identity.Client.dll` and `Azure.Core.dll` also contain IMDS endpoints, but the CLI configures the exporter with a connection string, so I believe the exporter's VM metadata lookup is the request being made. Refusing that address in a preload shim, with nothing else changed, brings the command from 2.02 s to 0.02 s.

## Expected behavior

A CLI command shouldn't wait on cloud-VM detection. Skipping the VM metadata lookup in the CLI's exporter configuration, or not blocking process exit on it, would remove the delay for anyone whose network drops packets to `169.254.169.254` rather than rejecting them.

## Related

- #54282: the same symptom on Windows with preview 4, caused by the OTLP exporter and fixed by disabling it by default in #54193. The OTLP exporter isn't involved here: the trace shows no connection to a local collector.
- #55184: discussion of the Azure Monitor exporter's fit for short-lived CLI processes.
Issues.RelatedDescription: Closed issue "Every dotnet command waits 2 s on SDK 11 RC2/RC3 (Linux): the telemetry exporter's Azure VM metadata request to 169.254.169.254 times out" (#56928)

Issues.Title: Fix culture-sensitive analyzer path resolution in ResolvePackageAssets
Issues.Body:
## Summary

Fix culture-sensitive analyzer path resolution in ResolvePackageAssets.

When resolving Roslyn analyzer assets from NuGet packages, AnalyzerResolver.IsFileCompilerVersionSpecific attempts to parse compiler version subfolders (e.g. `/roslyn5.0/`) using `file.IndexOf(_compilerNameSearchString)`. Because no `StringComparison` was specified, it defaulted to `StringComparison.CurrentCulture` (linguistic search).

In cultures where `/` is treated as ignorable punctuation (such as Thai `th-TH`), `file.IndexOf("/roslyn")` skips the leading slash and matches at `r`, offsetting the version start index by 1 character. Subsequently, `file.IndexOf('/', compilerVersionStart)` starts searching from `.` (also ignorable punctuation in Thai collation), immediately matching at offset 0 and returning an empty string `""`.

As a result, `Version.TryParse("")` returns `false`, causing the SDK to treat all compiler-specific analyzers as version-agnostic and pass every Roslyn variant (`roslyn4.0` through `roslyn5.0`) to the compiler simultaneously, leading to `CS0111` / `CS0757` compilation errors on machines running under such cultures.

Specifying `StringComparison.Ordinal` ensures technical path delimiter matching is consistent across all machine cultures.

\\\diff
- int compilerNameStart = file.IndexOf(_compilerNameSearchString);
+ int compilerNameStart = file.IndexOf(_compilerNameSearchString, StringComparison.Ordinal);
\\\

## Evidence

- **Before (`th-TH` culture):**
  - `file.IndexOf("/roslyn")` -> offset 10 instead of 9 (ignorable `/`)
  - `compilerVersionStart` -> offset 17 (pointing at `.`)
  - `file.IndexOf('/', 17)` -> matches immediately at 17 (ignorable `.` and `/` collision in linguistic collation)
  - Extracted version substring -> `""` (Length 0)
  - `Version.TryParse("")` fails -> All analyzer variants (`roslyn4.0` .. `roslyn5.0`) loaded -> Build fails with `CS0111`
- **After:**
  - `file.IndexOf("/roslyn", StringComparison.Ordinal)` -> offset 9
  - `compilerVersionStart` -> offset 16 (pointing at `5`)
  - `file.IndexOf('/', 16)` -> offset 19
  - Extracted version substring -> `"5.0"`
  - `Version.TryParse("5.0")` succeeds -> Only the highest compatible Roslyn analyzer is selected.

## Merge Danger

**Door:** two-way
**Blast Radius:** low (internal path resolution helper; technical paths must always use Ordinal string comparison per .NET runtime guidelines).
Issues.RelatedDescription: Open PR "Fix culture-sensitive analyzer path resolution in ResolvePackageAssets" (#56931)

Issues.Title: --coverage-output flag silently omits/deletes output files when solution has multiple test projects
Issues.Body:
### Describe the bug

If `dotnet test --coverage` is run with the flag `--coverage-output` in a solution with multiple test projects, there will be a report from only one of the test projects

### Steps to reproduce

1. Create a solution with two test projects using MTP
2. Run `dotnet test --coverage --coverage-output-format cobertura --coverage-output my-output-file.xml `
3. Inspect the output

Minimal demo: https://github.com/computaserik/CoverageOutputDemo/tree/main

### Expected behavior

`dotnet test` should fail, or at least issue a clear warning that output will be missing.

### Actual behavior

The test reports from all but one of the projects are silently omitted/deleted.

### Is this a regression?

_No response_

### Are there any workarounds?

Remove the `--coverage-output` option.

Issues.Title: dotnetup: support daily builds in admin mode (including RTM and servicing build identity)
Issues.Body:
## Summary

`dotnetup` admin mode (Windows installer bundles) cannot install daily builds today. It is expected to gain daily build support, and when it does, RTM and servicing daily builds need the same build-identity handling that archive installs received in #56913.

## Current behavior

- Admin mode installs through `WindowsBundleArtifact`, which forces `RequireReleasesJsonSignature = true` ([WindowsBundleArtifact.cs](https://github.com/dotnet/sdk/blob/release/dnup/src/Installer/dotnetup.Library/WindowsInstaller/WindowsBundleArtifact.cs)).
- Daily channels resolve only from the public blob feed, and that path calls `ThrowIfReleasesJsonSignatureRequired`, which fails with `AdminModeSignatureRequired` ([DotnetDownloader.cs](https://github.com/dotnet/sdk/blob/release/dnup/src/Installer/Microsoft.Dotnet.Installation/Internal/DotnetDownloader.cs)).
- `ResolveManifestEntry_RequestExpectsReleasesJsonSignature_RejectsUnsignedSource` in `DotnetDownloaderBlobFeedTests` asserts this for bundle requests.

So `dotnetup sdk install 11-daily` in admin mode fails before any download.

## Work needed

1. Decide how admin mode trusts daily bundles. They are not covered by the signed releases.json; Authenticode verification of the `.exe` may be enough (related: #54278).
2. Allow bundle requests through the blob feed path when that trust model is satisfied.

## Context: RTM and servicing daily builds (from #56913)

RTM and servicing daily builds live in a build-identity directory (for example `Sdk/11.0.100-rtm.26552.115/`) but publish files named with the release version (`dotnet-sdk-11.0.100-win-x64.exe`) and install into the release-version folder (`sdk/11.0.100`). #56913 handles this for archives. For bundles:

**Already handled**
- The blob feed fallback to the untagged file name also covers `.exe`, and `WindowsBundleArtifact.ProductVersion` passes the on-disk version through, so post-install validation and `--update-global-json` should use `11.0.100`.

**Gaps to address**
- **False "already installed".** Bundle installs decide "already installed" by validating the `sdk/11.0.100` folder. A different build in that folder (the stable release, or another RTM daily) is reported as already installed. Archive installs avoid this by comparing the commit on line 1 of each `.version` file in the archive with the folder on disk ([#56913, aa10c7e](https://github.com/dotnet/sdk/pull/56913/commits/aa10c7e4e2d56c90dc140e0bfb1dce9a457d93c3)). Bundles do not expose those files without extracting.
- **Windows Installer behavior is unverified.** Two different builds with the same product version (for example `11.0.100` RTM daily vs `11.0.100` release) may be treated as the same product by Windows Installer, resulting in a no-op or repair instead of the requested build. This needs to be tested.

**Possible approach**
- Compare the existing folder's `.version` commit (first line) with the requested build's commit. The commit for a daily build could come from the blob feed (for example `productCommit-<rid>.txt`), so the check would not depend on extracting the bundle.
- Verified facts on `.version`: SDK files contain commit / version / RID / full build version / feature band; runtime, ASP.NET Core and Windows Desktop files contain commit / version. A stable release is a promoted daily build, so its commit equals that daily's commit, and runtimes bundled in later SDK feature bands keep the 1xx build's commit.

## Related

- #56913: RTM and servicing daily build support for archive installs
- #56921: automatically replacing installs that share an on-disk version
- #56670: original daily install failure

Issues.Title: dotnetup: UX enhancement - automatically replace installs that share an on-disk version, with in-use detection
Issues.Body:
Follow-up from https://github.com/dotnet/sdk/pull/56913#discussion_r4461189250.

## Problem

RTM and servicing daily builds have a build identity such as `11.0.100-rtm.26552.115` but install under the untagged release version, for example `sdk/11.0.100`. Successive daily builds therefore share one on-disk folder, as does a stable `11.0.100` install.

After #56913, dotnetup detects this conflict and fails with a message telling the user to uninstall the owning install spec first. `dotnetup sdk update` for an RTM or servicing daily channel then needs a manual uninstall for every new build. This issue tracks doing the replacement automatically.

## Proposal

When a tracked install's on-disk folder belongs to a different build identity:

1. **Ask before replacing.** In interactive mode, show which install and which install specs will be replaced and ask for confirmation. In non-interactive mode, keep the current error unless an explicit opt-in is passed (for example `--replace` or `--yes`).
2. **Only replace what dotnetup owns.** Replace the folder only when every manifest record that uses it can be removed: records owned solely by the spec being updated, or specs the user confirmed. Never replace an untracked folder or one that a global.json spec still needs, unless the user explicitly confirms it.
3. **Replace atomically, and fail if files are in use.** Run under the install-state mutex:
   - Rename each affected folder to a sibling temp name, for example `sdk/.11.0.100.replacing-<guid>`. On failure, roll back any renames already done and report which folder is in use.
   - Extract the new payload into the original path.
   - On success, delete the renamed folders. If deletion fails, leave them for the garbage collector. On failure, restore them.
   - Update the manifest: remove the replaced records and add the new one.
4. **Cover bundled subcomponents.** An SDK archive also writes `shared/Microsoft.NETCore.App/<v>`, `shared/Microsoft.AspNetCore.App/<v>`, `host/fxr/<v>`, and packs. Today the extractor skips subcomponents that already exist, so a stale runtime from build A survives an update to build B. Before commit, list the archive's subcomponents. Treat each existing subcomponent owned by a different build identity as part of the same replacement set.

## In-use detection: needs investigation

Checking only the muxer isn't enough, because SDK and framework DLLs can also be in use.

- **Windows (NTFS):** renaming a directory fails when any file inside is open without `FILE_SHARE_DELETE`. Loaded DLLs and running executables are usually open that way. The rename test from step 3 should therefore be a reliable all-or-nothing check. Verify this with: a running `dotnet build` server (MSBuild node reuse), `dotnet watch`, a running app using the shared framework, the VS Code C# extension, and files opened by antivirus.
- **Linux, macOS and WSL (ext4 and similar):** renaming succeeds even while files are in use, because running processes keep the old inodes and continue on the old build. A rename can't detect use, though replacing is safe for running processes. Options:
  - Scan `/proc/*/maps` and `/proc/*/fd` for paths under the folder (Linux and WSL only; incomplete for other users' processes without privileges).
  - Accept replacement while files are in use and print a warning.
  - Use an advisory lock file that dotnetup-launched processes hold.
- **WSL on DrvFs (`/mnt/c/...`):** paths on the Windows drive behave differently from ext4, and a rename may fail like on Windows. Test both.
- **macOS:** behaves like Linux, but there's no `/proc`. Would need `lsof` or `proc_pidinfo`, or acceptance of replacement while in use.

Also decide whether `dotnetup` should hold a shared lock while running `dotnet` through `dotnetup dotnet`, so replacement can wait for or detect those processes.

## Tests

- Update build A to build B, both sharing a folder: the files and the manifest end up matching build B.
- Stable `11.0.100` already installed, then an RTM daily: prompt or error, and the stable install is untouched unless confirmed.
- A file inside the folder is held open (Windows): the replacement fails, the original folder is restored, and the manifest is unchanged.
- Non-interactive mode without the opt-in: the current error is unchanged.
- A bundled runtime subcomponent owned by a different build identity is replaced or reported.

## Related

- #56670: the original RTM daily install failure
- #56913: adds the conflict error this issue would replace
- #55311: dotnetup should not uninstall an SDK that is in use

Issues.Title: Hot Reload startup hook blocks app forever before Main when host handshake never completes (Visual Studio + Aspire)
Issues.Body:
### Describe the bug

When an Aspire AppHost is started with F5 in Visual Studio, one child project (an ASP.NET Core Blazor Server app) never reaches Main. The process is alive and the debugger is attached, but its main thread is blocked inside the Hot Reload startup hook (Listener.Listen -> InitializeAsync(...).GetAwaiter().GetResult()). There is no timeout, log output, warning or exception, so the app waits forever. Aspire shows the resource as "Running (Unhealthy)".

Turning off "Enable Hot Reload" in Visual Studio makes the project start normally, so the hang is caused by the Hot Reload handshake.

### Steps to reproduce

I don't have a minimal repro yet. What I do:

1. Open a solution with an Aspire AppHost (Aspire 13.6.4) containing a SQL database, a simple ASP.NET Core mock project, and the affected Blazor Server project as project resources.
2. In Tools > Options > Debugging > .NET/C++ Hot Reload, have "Enable Hot Reload" on.
3. Start the AppHost with F5 (debugger attached).
4. The affected project shows "Running (Unhealthy)" in the Aspire dashboard and never logs anything.
5. A breakpoint on the first line of Program.cs is never hit.
6. Use Debug > Break All, select the affected process, and look at its main thread: it is blocked in the Hot Reload startup hook.

The other project in the same AppHost starts fine with the same settings. The affected project also starts fine when run on its own from Visual Studio.

### Expected behavior

If the handshake with the Hot Reload host doesn't complete, the agent should time out and either log a warning and continue without Hot Reload, or fail with a clear error. A project shouldn't be able to hang indefinitely before Main with no diagnostics.

### Actual behavior

The app never starts. StartupHook.Initialize calls listener.Listen(CancellationToken.None), and Listen blocks on:

    // block execution of the app until initial updates are applied:
    InitializeAsync(cancellationToken).GetAwaiter().GetResult();

There is no timeout and it can't be cancelled. If the host never sends InitialUpdatesCompleted, the app waits forever.

Main thread stack (innermost first):

    [Managed to Native Transition]
    Monitor.Wait
    ManualResetEventSlim.Wait
    Task.SpinThenBlockingWait
    Task.InternalWaitCore
    Task.InternalWait
    TaskAwaiter.HandleNonSuccessAndDebuggerNotification
    [Waiting on Async Operation]
    Microsoft.DotNet.HotReload.Listener.Listen(CancellationToken)   Line 38
    StartupHook.Initialize()                                        Line 99
    MethodBaseInvoker.InvokeWithNoArgs
    StartupHookProvider.CallStartupHook
    StartupHookProvider.ProcessStartupHooks

The process loads the same modules as the working project up to System.Security.Claims.dll (Microsoft.Extensions.DotNetDeltaApplier.dll, System.IO.Pipes), then nothing more. Microsoft.AspNetCore.dll is never loaded, and a temporary File.WriteAllText as the first line of Program.cs never creates its file.

### Is this a regression?

Unknown. I haven't tested other Visual Studio, SDK or Aspire versions. I'm adding Aspire to an existing app, so I have no earlier working state under Aspire.

### Are there any workarounds?

Yes: turn off "Enable Hot Reload" in Tools > Options > Debugging > .NET/C++ Hot Reload. The project then starts and runs normally under Aspire. This disables Hot Reload for every project, though.

### Other details

- Aspire AppHost 13.6.4, .NET runtime 10.0.9.
- Not yet determined: which await in InitializeAsync is pending (SendAsync or ReceiveAndApplyUpdatesAsync), which transport is in use, and why the host doesn't complete the handshake for this project but does for the other one in the same AppHost. The host side is Visual Studio, so this may need a Developer Community report too.
- Related: dotnet/sdk#54023 fixes a deadlock in the same call chain on iOS, caused by a SynchronizationContext installed before startup hooks run. I don't believe that applies here, since no synchronization context is expected on this app's main thread, but the blocking pattern is the same.
- I have a minidump of the hung process. It contains secrets, so I'm not attaching it, but I can share it privately if asked.

## Summary
Backport only the two `ProjectUpdateInProcTests` completion-wait fixes from https://github.com/dotnet/sdk/pull/53424 (commit 96683a0ad81c5694820f7824342a4ca5079bdd64) to `release/10.0.4xx`.

Issues.Title: Support RTM daily builds in `dotnetup`
Issues.Body: ## Summary Fixes https://github.com/dotnet/sdk/issues/56670. RTM builds retain their build identity in the feed directory but publish archives with an untagged product-version filename. For example, the `11.0.1xx-daily` shortlink resolves to: ```text https://ci.dot.net/public/Sdk/11.0.100-rtm.26552.115/dotnet-sdk-11.0.100-osx-arm64.tar.gz ``` Dotnetup tried to use `dotnet-sdk-11.0.100-rtm.26552.115-osx-arm64.tar.gz`, whose checksum does not exist. # Complications The RTM versions extract their layout onto the same versioned folder as the full GA release, so both `11.0.100-rtm.26552.115` and `11.0.100` use `11.0.100` for the on-disk layout. This means that only one can exist at a time per dotnet root. The `.version` file must be read to actually determine the version, and this is also true for the .NET Runtime installs. Overlay / install exist checks become more complicated due to this, as the reasoning against folder names no longer always holds true. This is also true when a .NET SDK RTM version is tracked in the manifest, and we want to install a different RTM/GA Runtime, where the versions may not match but we have to demystify the install state to avoid incorrect behavior. # This change: - Tries the product-version filename in the same build-specific directory only after the original checksum returns 404. - Carries the payload product version through verified downloads and installation artifacts. The tracked version remains the build identity, so daily updates can distinguish successive builds. - Records optional `productVersion` metadata only when the on-disk version differs. Post-install validation, stale-entry pruning, verified listing, and update checks use it. Existing manifests without this property retain their current behavior. - Documents why `dotnet --version` can report a release version for an RTM or servicing daily build. - Checks global.json and uses the "Product Version" in global.json rather than the RTM version, as global.json doesn't work with the RTM versions as a version string. - Compares install specs and existing installs using `.version` files, considering that the folder name containing the 'version' is no longer semantically correct - Fails with an error if you try to install two different installs that share the same directory components: To reduce scope, this is the proposed behavior. https://github.com/dotnet/sdk/issues/56921 tracks future behavior which could be interactive automated removal of the blocking install with e2e replacement of the newer RTM version. - Note that '11.0.100' still is not accepted as an RTM value because it is not released yet. 11-daily or 11.0.1xx-daily must be used. This is the correct behavior in my mind, because 11.0.100 is the official release, not the RTM release.
Issues.RelatedDescription: Open PR "Support RTM daily builds in `dotnetup`" (#56913)

Issues.Title: Preserve invocation context during MTP strict-MT preparation
Issues.Body:
Strict-MT MTP preparation owns the process current directory until its MSBuild session ends. Parent-side operations must retain the invocation directory: otherwise background workload updates can miss repository `global.json` and `NuGet.Config`, and relative `DOTNET_CLI_TEST_TRACEFILE` paths can produce caught I/O exceptions and `MSB4287` while `dotnet test` exits successfully without the requested trace.

Capture the invocation directory before scheduling background updates and forward it through workload manifest discovery and the existing NuGet downloader override. Normalize and cache the trace path before managed MTP preparation starts. This preserves main's public `CommandServices` constructor contract, file-based execution, and strict-MT directory ownership without disabling updates or weakening MSBuild checks.

Follow-up to #56893. The matching release backport is #56908.

## Validation

- Managed CLI, shared-AOT compilation, and test builds passed with zero warnings or errors. Native publishing and native execution were not run.
- **75 focused cases passed, 0 failed, 0 skipped**, including workload configuration/local-feed lookup, trace logging, main's file-based no-build MT/legacy paths, `CommandServices` propagation, preparation failures, and multi-project/multi-TFM binlogs.

Issues.Title: Optimized NativeAOT publish skips runtime configuration hooks, breaking System.CommandLine executable-name injection
Issues.Body:
### Description

Updating from SDK `11.0.100-rc.1.26425.128` to `11.0.100-rc.2.26504.105` breaks System.CommandLine’s NativeAOT shared-library test on Windows, macOS, and Linux.

The optimized publish path introduced by dotnet/sdk#54515 skips `GenerateBuildRuntimeConfigurationFiles`. System.CommandLine contributes a runtime configuration item through this hook:

```xml
<Target Name="_AddSystemCommandLineExecutableName"
        DependsOnTargets="PrepareForBuild"
        BeforeTargets="GenerateBuildRuntimeConfigurationFiles">
  <ItemGroup>
    <RuntimeHostConfigurationOption
        Include="System.CommandLine.ExecutableName"
        Value="$(AssemblyName)"
        Trim="false" />
  </ItemGroup>
</Target>
```

Because the target no longer executes, the item never reaches NativeAOT’s compiler and is not embedded in the native image. The library publishes and loads successfully, but its executable name falls back to `dotnet` on Windows and `app` on macOS/Linux instead of `NativeLibrary`.

### Reproduction and evidence

The existing integration test in dotnet/command-line-api#2847 reproduces this by publishing a NativeAOT shared library and invoking an exported function that returns `new RootCommand().Name`.

- [Passing build with RC1](https://dev.azure.com/dnceng-public/public/_build/results?buildId=1640186)
- [Failing build with RC2](https://dev.azure.com/dnceng-public/public/_build/results?buildId=1643661)
- [Root-cause investigation](https://github.com/dotnet/command-line-api/pull/2847#issuecomment-6320900266)
- [System.CommandLine target at the failing revision](https://github.com/dotnet/command-line-api/blob/f894530bfd984e4ffeb53f1ec9e774b1409cb775/src/System.CommandLine/build/System.CommandLine.targets#L11-L25)

The tested revisions differ only in SDK/Arcade versions and dependency metadata.

### Expected behavior

Runtime configuration contributed by package targets remains available to NativeAOT publishing, or packages receive documented guidance identifying the supported hook replacing `GenerateBuildRuntimeConfigurationFiles`.

### Workaround

The SDK documents `UseOptimizedPublish=false` as the opt-out restoring the full build path.

Verified locally on macOS with SDK `12.0.100-alpha.1.26516.101`: after adding `<UseOptimizedPublish>false</UseOptimizedPublish>` to the NativeLibrary test project, the targeted Release integration test passed (1 passed, 0 failed, 0 skipped):

```sh
dotnet test src/System.CommandLine.Tests/System.CommandLine.Tests.csproj -c Release -f net10.0 --filter FullyQualifiedName~RootCommand_name_falls_back_to_the_AppContext_value_when_hosted_as_a_native_library --no-restore
```

This validates the workaround on the local SDK; it has not yet been rerun on the original RC2 SDK or Windows/Linux.

### Related

 dotnet/sdk#56645 and dotnet/sdk#56649 address another consequence of the optimized publish path. That ordering fix does not restore `GenerateBuildRuntimeConfigurationFiles` or this hook.
